tspan.tspan: Data analysis
Organohalides
are pervasive environmental pollutants commonly
found in contaminated soil and groundwater, causing serious harm to
ecological stability and human health. Because traditional removal
approaches pose a large economic and environmental burden, more
sustainable practices have emerged, especially bioremediation.
Bioremediation
enhances natural microbial communities, which can
partially degrade organohalides such as organochlorines, by enriching
the existing strains or inoculating new specialised ones. While long
established, bioremediation has not yet benefitted from the recent
advances in computational
predictive modelling
and microbiome
data science.
In this project, we will develop
machine learning
methods to predict
in-situ
organohalide biodegradation rates from microbiome profiles at
a well-studied contaminated site in Australia, to ultimately reduce the
uncertainty over bioremediation project performance.
The
BIP data
includes groundwater chemical conditions, contaminant
concentrations, and 16S rRNA gene sequencing data from multiple
monitoring locations for over 20 years. Sample biochemical properties
vary based on time, plume type, and collection depth. The time-series
setup also allows for predicting future degradation trajectories.
Leveraging the
R/Bioconductor
ecosystem for microbiome data science
[3], informative ecological features will be generated from the input
counts table, enhanced with prior functional knowledge derived from
selected public databases, such as metabolic pathways and microbial co-
occurrence networks.
The generated features will be used to cross-validate different model
categories (regression, tree-based, foundational and neural network)
and predict contaminant
degradation rates
over time. For
in-silico
microbiome optimisation, a reversed pipeline could predict optimal
microbial compositions based on contaminant concentrations.
This project has received support from the Australian Government
Research Training Program Scholarship and funding from the Australian
Research Counci
l (decision LP240200954) and the Research Council of
